title: Optimize response serialization and prune legacy cache adapters
creator: Ava Kim
description:
Background: The console backend aggregation layer currently performs multiple passes of response normalization and serialization across GraphQL resolvers and the HTTP response path. This duplicated work increases p50/p95 response CPU and allocs, contributes to GC churn, and interacts poorly with our legacy cache adapters (old in-memory LRU shim + redis-compat wrapper) which make defensive copies of payloads.

Goal: Reduce CPU and allocation overhead in the console hotpath by consolidating serialization/normalization into a single pipeline stage, removing duplicate object cloning, and phasing out the legacy cache adapter stack in favor of the unified cache adapter introduced in ENG-128990. Target measurable improvements: ~>15% decrease in p50 and p95 CPU and a 10-20% reduction in p95 tail latency for aggregated API endpoints under realistic load.

Scope: This ticket covers changes in the console aggregation service and its GraphQL/REST handlers only. It does NOT include the frontend rendering layer or unrelated microservices. Work items include: 1) Introduce a single canonical response buffer used by resolvers; 2) Replace ad-hoc serializer utilities with the shared serializer; 3) Remove legacy cache adapter registration and migrate callers to the unified cache adapter; 4) Upgrade graphql-js to v18 to pick up performance fixes and make resolver execution hooks consistent (see technical notes).
acceptance_criteria: Aggregated API endpoints show >=15% reduction in CPU tokenized p50 under benchmark harness compared to baseline (see dashboard link)
No increased error rates in staging for 72h of canary traffic (error budget check)
Unit and integration tests cover serialization pipeline and cache adapter feature flags
Rollout gated behind feature flag 'unified-serializer-v1' with automatic rollback on SLA breach
Legacy cache adapter code paths removed and compilation warnings cleaned up; no runtime references remain
technical_notes: Canonical buffer: add RequestContext.responseBuffer (owned per-request) that resolvers write into instead of creating intermediate JS objects repeatedly.

Serializer consolidation: centralize stringify/escape logic into packages/console-serializer with deterministic field ordering for stable caching. Expose two APIs: serializeForCache(payload) and serializeForWire(payload).
Cache migration: de-register legacy adapters at startup via feature flag; adapt existing cache keys to use new stable serialization format (migration script included).

GraphQL upgrade: bump graphql-js to v18.2.1 — requires small resolver typing adjustments and replacing deprecated execute() call sites. Benchmarked locally with no semantic regressions on test queries.
Memory safety: avoid Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(...)) on hotpath; prefer incremental serializer that writes to pre-sized buffer when content-length can be estimated.
Fallbacks: when 'unified-serializer-v1' is false, system retains current behavior. Add metrics to measure delta between old/new code paths (serializer.vs.old.*).
Compatibility: ensure serializeForCache produces stable output for existing cache keys for 30 days to allow cold cache during rollout; after 30 days we will rotate keys by appending 'v2'.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag with unit tests and canary PRs (small percentage traffic in staging)
2) Run benchmark harness (k6 + local replay) comparing old vs new under 50/100/200 concurrency and capture CPU/alloc/latency
3) Canary in production at 1% traffic for 2 hours, monitor error rate, p50/p95 latency, CPU and GC metrics
4) If stable, increase to 10% for 6 hours, then 50% for 12 hours, then full rollout
5) If SLA or error budget breach detected during any stage, toggle feature flag off and roll back; collect heap/profile artifacts for postmortem
